questions.q: Using $r = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}$: if $\text{Cov}(X, Y) = 6$, $\sigma_X = 2$ and $\sigma_Y = 5$, what is $r$?
questions.explain: $r = 6/(2 \times 5) = 0.6$, a moderate positive trend. $r$ must lie in $[-1, 1]$, so $6$ and $1.2$ are impossible.

questions.q: Temperature in °C vs. the same temperature in °F ($F = 1.8\,C + 32$). What is Pearson $r$?
questions.explain: The points lie exactly on an increasing straight line, so $r = 1$. $r$ measures how tightly points hug a line, not the slope — the 1.8 and 32 are irrelevant.

questions.q: Points lie exactly on a symmetric U-shaped curve, so X determines Y. What is the Pearson correlation?
options: $0$ (or near $0$), because there is no *linear* trend
questions.explain: Pearson $r$ only measures linear association. The symmetric U has no overall upward or downward trend, so the least-squares line is flat and $r \approx 0$ — never trust $r$ without plotting.

questions.q: One variable is constant ($\sigma_Y = 0$). What is $r$?
questions.explain: The covariance is $0$ and the denominator $\sigma_X \cdot 0$ is also $0$, so $r = 0/0$ is undefined — not zero.
